title: Identifying NYC Parks with Vehicle Traffic
text:
Parks Properties
The Parks Properties dataset description carries the caveat:

This dataset identifies property managed partially or solely by NYC Parks. This data has been produced in whole or part using secondary data. Data accuracy is limited by the scale and accuracy of the original sources. Site-specific conditions should be field-verified. 

At least two ambiguities are described above. One is the official-unofficial nature of the data. It’s provided to NYC Open Data by the Department of Parks, but it’s comprised of secondary data (at least in part, or maybe in whole – another ambiguity. Does the Department of Parks not know what properties are under their jurisdiction?). The other is that it’s unclear what types of properties are included in the dataset. Are they all parks? A mixture of parks and something else? We can take a look at the unique combinations of class, subcategory, and typecategory:


Code
invisible(
  property_types <- soc_read(
    "https://data.cityofnewyork.us/Recreation/Parks-Properties/enfh-gkve.json",
    query = soc_query(
      select = "distinct class, subcategory, typecategory"
    )
  )
)

PARK is the only class of property in the dataset. Based on the combinations of subcategory and typecategory, it may be possible to determine which properties may be excluded from our list of parks, but for now we’ll consider each feature in the dataset to be a park.

title: Identifying NYC Parks with Vehicle Traffic
text:
NYC Street Centerline
The centerline dataset is described as:

The NYC Street Centerline (CSCL) is a road-bed representation of New York City streets containing address ranges and other information such as traffic directions, road types, segment types.

This brief description implies that this dataset is entirely composed of streets, i.e. surfaces for vehicles to travel. However, taking a look at the rw_type reveals that not to be the case2:


Code
street_types <- property_types <- soc_read(
  "https://data.cityofnewyork.us/City-Government/Centerline/inkn-q76z.json",
  query = soc_query(
    select = "distinct rw_type"
  )
)

street_types <- street_types |> 
  mutate(`Roadway Type` = case_when(
    rw_type == 1 ~ "Street",
    rw_type == 2 ~ "Highway",
    rw_type == 3 ~ "Bridge",
    rw_type == 4 ~ "Tunnel",
    rw_type == 5 ~ "Boardwalk",
    rw_type == 6 ~ "Path/Trail",
    rw_type == 7 ~ "StepStreet",
    rw_type == 8 ~ "Driveway",
    rw_type == 9 ~ "Ramp",
    rw_type == 10 ~ "Alley",
    rw_type == 11 ~ "Unknown",
    rw_type == 12 ~ "Non-Physical Street Segment",
    rw_type == 13 ~ "U Turn",
    rw_type == 14 ~ "Ferry Route",
  ))

street_types |>
  arrange(rw_type) |>
  mutate(rw_type = as.character(rw_type)) |>
  cil_table(widths = c(15, 85),
            unit = "%")



rw_typeRoadway Type1Street2Highway3Bridge4Tunnel5Boardwalk6Path/Trail7StepStreet8Driveway9Ramp10Alley12Non-Physical Street Segment13U Turn14Ferry Route


We’ll want to exclude segments where rw_type is 6 to keep paths/trails from counting as a site for vehicular traffic. It’s possible that other roadway types should be excluded, but for now, only Path/Trail will be.

The report is published, with a list of 481 parks
September 15, 2026
Tags: Site, Data
In answer to a request from New Yorkers for Parks, the report lists NYC parks that appear to let cars drive through them: every park that contains a road segment cars can use, except Central Park and Prospect Park. It finds 481 of 2,059 parks, and says the list includes some parks that do not belong and needs to be checked by hand. The list can be downloaded as a spreadsheet (CSV) and as a map file (GeoJSON). Wording edits and a source note for the City's street map data followed the same day.
